items.readable_text:
Content:
We are often interested in understanding how functions behave as their input becomes very large or very small. This is called the function's end behavior.

Content:
Consider the function [MATH: y=f(x)] below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/f5242b0f9cab6363890ee812ad15420b]

Content:
The key to understanding the end behavior is to ask the following two questions:

Content:
1. What is the graph doing as [MATH: x] becomes very large? ([MATH: x \to \infty])
2. What is the graph doing as [MATH: x] becomes very small? ([MATH: x \to -\infty])

Content:
Let's now answer these questions.

Content:
- First, consider [MATH: x \to \infty.] On the right of the graph, as [MATH: x] gets larger and larger, the function value "levels off" to [MATH: 1.] In other words, as [MATH: x] approaches "infinity," [MATH: f(x)] approaches [MATH: 1.]

We can express this using mathematical notation as follows:
[MATH: f(x) \rightarrow 1 \quad \text{as} \quad x\rightarrow \infty]

[IMG: /graphics/a9cb10184dd29d07d7ca8804cccd0ff1]
- Now, consider [MATH: x \to -\infty.] On the left of the graph, as [MATH: x] gets more and more negative, the function does not "level off." Instead, the value of [MATH: f(x)] grows larger and larger without bound. In other words, as [MATH: x] approaches "negative infinity," [MATH: f(x)] approaches "infinity."

We can express this using mathematical notation as follows:
[MATH: f(x) \rightarrow \infty \quad \text{as} \quad x\rightarrow -\infty]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/72fba1dcaa3c8aabafabc8d21c8bef5c]

Content:
When determining a function's end behavior, we ignore anything happening in the middle of the graph, as this is irrelevant to a function's end behavior.

Content:
If the graph "levels off" in any of the two cases above, we've found a horizontal asymptote! In the example above, [MATH: y=1] is a horizontal asymptote.

Content:
More formally, whenever [MATH: f(x)] approaches some finite number [MATH: a] as [MATH: x \rightarrow -\infty] or [MATH: x \rightarrow \infty,] we say that [MATH: y=a] is a horizontal asymptote of the function [MATH: y=f(x).]

1. [MATH: y=2] is a horizontal asymptote of [MATH: f(x)]
2. [MATH: f(x) \rightarrow -1] as [MATH: x \rightarrow -\infty]
3. [MATH: y=0] is a horizontal asymptote of [MATH: f(x)]

[IMG: /graphics/258cbe02d90a3d4586a68aede30d6b79]

sections.normalized_html:
Let's analyze each statement one-by-one.

  • On the right side of the graph, we see that as [MATH: x] gets larger and larger, the function [MATH: f(x)] levels off to the value of [MATH: 2.] Symbolically, [MATH: f(x) \to 2 \quad \text{as} \quad x \rightarrow \infty.] This means that [MATH: y=2] is a horizontal asymptote of [MATH: f.] Therefore, I is true.

  • On the left side of the graph, we see that as [MATH: x] gets more and more negative, the function [MATH: f(x)] levels off to the value of [MATH: -1.] Symbolically, [MATH: f(x) \to -1 \quad \text{as} \quad x \to -\infty.] Therefore, II is also true.

  • The horizontal asymptotes of [MATH: f(x)] are [MATH: y=2] and [MATH: y=-1]. The line [MATH: y=0] is not a horizontal asymptote because the function does not level off to [MATH: 0] on the right nor on the left. Therefore, III is false.

As a result, the correct answer is "I and II only".
